newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy vows federal reform, Bossi insults the press.
newsitem.headline: Italy vows federal reform, Bossi insults the press.

text.p: Italy's government pledged to press on with federal reform on Monday, acknowledging that separatist Umberto Bossi remained a threat to unity despite his failure to draw mass support for a weekend "declaration of independence".

The Italian media portrayed Bossi's breakaway bid as a fiasco but the abrasive Northern League leader remained unbowed and prompted a mass walk-out at a news conference in Milan when he insulted a journalist and accused the media of lying.

"We don't tolerate those who come from outside to dirty our people. You are a foot-licker of the system," he railed at Ersilia Carbone, from state radio RAI, when she asked why children had apparently joined in Sunday's "independence" vote.
Regional Affairs Minister Franco Bassanini said Bossi had drawn fewer than 150,000 to his three days of rallies along the River Po, but Bossi insisted 1.5 million turned out.

"The fact that the Northern League flopped doesn't mean that the need for reform has become any less urgent," Bassanini told a news conference a day after Bossi's symbolic proclamation of a "federal republic of Padania" in the elegant city of Venice.

He said the centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi, which is already working on two packages of laws giving local authorities more say in administration and taxation, would forge ahead towards constitutional reform and federalism.

Unless Italy enacted institutional reforms aimed at more local autonomy and a streamlined bureaucracy there was "a risk that a separatist programme would be embraced out of desperation by those who really don't want it," Bassanini said.
"The road ahead is that of federalist reform."
A parliamentary commission is to have two years to work out constitutional reform aimed at giving Italy a federal structure. After it is approved by parliament it will go to a referendum.
Bossi's demonstrations were far overshadowed by rival rallies in favour of Italian unity, but he refused to agree.
He called journalists "riff-raff" and said they could not care less about freedom of information and were only bothered about protecting their jobs and furthering their careers.
Although the media judged Bossi's would-be state "Padania" a non-starter, commentators said the fundamental grievances of many northerners were still to be resolved.
Many in the industrial north say institutions they perceive as corrupt, a centralised government, and high taxes to fund an incompetent bureaucracy are at the base of their complaints.
Bossi, who says the rich north is being held back by a corrupt, Mafia-ridden south, has said federalism is no use and political analysts cautioned that separatism was far from dead.
"Declaring victory, as some 'Italian' politicians will, would be a mistake," said Sergio Romano in a front-page column in the leading northern daily newspaper La Stampa.
"If the opera is a comic one and the leading actor an uncontrollable ham, the gist of the libretto remains nonetheless serious and dramatic," Romano commented.
The Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano called Bossi's declaration "a deep wound and an outrage for the nation" but also warned that it would be "superficial" to write Bossi off.
In declaring independence Bossi said Padania was "a sovereign and independent federal republic" and announced a temporary constitution and provisional government.
The League also read out a 10-point "bill of rights for the citizens of Padania" in which the formation of a Padanian national guard was to be set up to defend the state.
